The amount of Martian deuterium (D/H = 9.3 ± 1.7 10−4) is five to seven times the amount on Earth (D/H = 1.56 10−4), suggesting that ancient Mars had significantly higher levels of water. Results from the ''Curiosity'' rover had previously found a high ratio of deuterium in [[Gale Crater]], though not significantly high enough to suggest the former presence of an ocean. Other scientists caution that these results have not been confirmed, and point out that Martian climate models have not yet shown that the planet was warm enough in the past to support bodies of liquid water.{{cite news |last=Kaufman |first=Marc |date=5 March 2015 |title=Mars Had an Ocean, Scientists Say, Pointing to New Data |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/03/06/science/mars-had-an-ocean-scientists-say-pointing-to-new-data.html |access-date=5 March 2015 |archive-date=7 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200307000937/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/03/06/science/mars-had-an-ocean-scientists-say-pointing-to-new-data.html |url-status=live}} Near the northern polar cap is the {{convert|81.4|km}} wide [[Korolev (Martian crater)|Korolev Crater]], which the [[Mars Express]] orbiter found to be filled with approximately {{convert|2200|km3}} of water ice.{{cite news |last1=Sample |first1=Ian |date=21 December 2018 |title=Mars Express beams back images of ice-filled Korolev crater |newspaper=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/dec/21/mars-express-beams-back-images-of-ice-filled-korolev-crater |access-date=21 December 2018 |archive-date=8 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208045902/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/dec/21/mars-express-beams-back-images-of-ice-filled-korolev-crater |url-status=live}} In November 2016, NASA reported finding a large amount of underground ice in the [[Utopia Planitia]] region. The volume of water detected has been estimated to be equivalent to the volume of water in [[Lake Superior]] (which is 12,100 cubic kilometers{{Cite web |date=29 October 2010 |title=EPA; Great Lakes; Physical Facts |url=http://www.epa.gov/glnpo/physfacts.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101029215637/http://www.epa.gov/glnpo/physfacts.html |archive-date=29 October 2010 |access-date=15 February 2023}}).{{cite web |date=22 November 2016 |title=Mars Ice Deposit Holds as Much Water as Lake Superior |url=http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?release=2016-299 |access-date=23 November 2016 |publisher=NASA |archive-date=26 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226060807/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/ |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}{{cite web |author=Staff |date=22 November 2016 |title=Scalloped Terrain Led to Finding of Buried Ice on Mars |url=http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA21136 |access-date=23 November 2016 |publisher=NASA |archive-date=26 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226060804/https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA21136%20 |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}} During observations from 2018 through 2021, the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter spotted indications of water, probably subsurface ice, in the Valles Marineris canyon system.{{Cite journal |last1=Mitrofanov |first1=I. |last2=Malakhov |first2=A. |last3=Djachkova |first3=M. |last4=Golovin |first4=D. |last5=Litvak |first5=M. |last6=Mokrousov |first6=M. |last7=Sanin |first7=A. |last8=Svedhem |first8=H. |last9=Zelenyi |first9=L. |date=March 2022 |title=The evidence for unusually high hydrogen abundances in the central part of Valles Marineris on Mars |journal=Icarus |volume=374 |article-number=114805 |bibcode=2022Icar..37414805M |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2021.114805 |s2cid=244449654 |doi-access=free}} == Orbital motion == {{Main|Orbit of Mars}} {{See also|Timekeeping on Mars}}{{Anchor|Viewing from Earth|Orbit and rotation}}[[File:Solar system orrery inner planets.gif|alt=Mars circling the Sun further and slower than Earth|thumb|upright=1.2|Orbit of Mars and other Inner Solar System planets]] Mars's average distance from the Sun is roughly {{convert|143|e6mi|e6km|abbr=unit|order=flip}}, and its orbital period is 687 (Earth) days. The solar day (or [[Mars sol|sol]]) on Mars is only slightly longer than an Earth day: 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35.244 seconds.{{cite book |last1=Badescu |first1=Viorel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BnPE37Ms5awC&pg=PA600 |title=Mars: Prospective Energy and Material Resources |date=2009 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-03629-3 |edition=illustrated |page=600 |access-date=20 May 2016 |archive-date=4 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230304004803/https://books.google.com/books?id=BnPE37Ms5awC&pg=PA600 |url-status=live}} A Martian year is equal to 1.8809 Earth years, or 1 year, 320 days, and 18.2 hours. The [[gravitational potential]] difference and thus the [[Delta-v budget|delta-v needed]] to transfer between Mars and Earth is the second lowest for Earth.{{cite journal |last1=Petropoulos |first1=Anastassios E. |last2=Longuski |first2=James M. |last3=Bonfiglio |first3=Eugene P. |year=2000 |title=Trajectories to Jupiter via Gravity Assists from Venus, Earth, and Mars |journal=Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets |publisher=American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA) |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=776–783 |bibcode=2000JSpRo..37..776P |doi=10.2514/2.3650 |issn=0022-4650}}{{cite web |last=Taylor |first=Chris |date=9 July 2020 |title=Welcome to Cloud City: The case for going to Venus, not Mars |url=https://mashable.com/feature/venus-mars-space-exploration |access-date=21 October 2022 |website=Mashable |archive-date=21 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021222623/https://mashable.com/feature/venus-mars-space-exploration |url-status=live}} The axial tilt of Mars is 25.19° relative to its [[orbital plane]], which is similar to the [[Ecliptic#Obliquity of the ecliptic|axial tilt of Earth]]. As a result, Mars has seasons like Earth, though on Mars they are nearly twice as long because its orbital period is that much longer. In the present day, the orientation of the [[north pole]] of Mars is close to the star [[Deneb]]. Mars has a relatively pronounced [[orbital eccentricity]] of about 0.09; of the seven other planets in the Solar System, only [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] has a larger orbital eccentricity. It is known that in the past, Mars has had a much more circular orbit. At one point, 1.35 million Earth years ago, Mars had an eccentricity of roughly 0.002, much less than that of Earth today. Mars's [[Milankovitch cycles|cycle of eccentricity]] is 96,000 Earth years compared to Earth's cycle of 100,000 years. Mars has its closest approach to Earth ([[opposition (astronomy)|opposition]]) in a [[synodic period]] of 779.94 days. It should not be confused with Mars [[conjunction (astronomy)|conjunction]], where the Earth and Mars are at opposite sides of the Solar System and form a straight line crossing the Sun. The average time between the successive oppositions of Mars, its synodic period, is 780 days; but the number of days between successive oppositions can range from 764 to 812. The distance at close approach varies between about {{convert|54|and|103|e6km|e6mi|abbr=unit}} due to the planets' [[ellipse|elliptical]] orbits, which causes comparable variation in [[angular size]]. At their furthest Mars and Earth can be as far as {{convert|401|e6km|e6mi|abbr=unit}} apart.{{cite web |last1=Tillman |first1=Nola Taylor |last2=Dobrijevic |first2=Daisy |title=How Long Does It Take to Get to Mars? |website=Space.com |date=20 January 2022 |url=https://www.space.com/24701-how-long-does-it-take-to-get-to-mars.html#:~:text=The%20two%20planets%20are%20farthest,miles%20(225%20million%20km). |access-date=23 August 2024}} Mars comes into opposition from Earth every 2.1 years. The planets come into opposition near Mars's [[perihelion]] in 2003, 2018 and 2035, with the 2020 and 2033 events being particularly close to perihelic opposition.{{cite web |title=Mars Opposition |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/night-sky/opposition |access-date=7 December 2021 |website=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |date=10 November 2017 |archive-date=5 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231005222312/https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/night-sky/opposition/ |url-status=live}}{{cite web |date=5 October 2021 |title=Why is Mars sometimes bright and sometimes faint? |url=https://earthsky.org/astronomy-essentials/why-is-mars-sometimes-bright-and-sometimes-faint/ |access-date=7 December 2021 |website=EarthSky |archive-date=7 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207122120/https://earthsky.org/astronomy-essentials/why-is-mars-sometimes-bright-and-sometimes-faint/ |url-status=live}}{{Cite web |date=3 November 2005 |title=Close encounter: Mars at opposition |url=https://www.spacetelescope.org/images/opo0534l/ |access-date=1 April 2022 |website=ESA/Hubble |archive-date=10 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910011439/http://www.spacetelescope.org/images/opo0534l/ |url-status=live}} [[File:Mars - 2020 Opposition (crop).jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|Mars seen through a 16-inch amateur telescope, at 2020 opposition]] The mean [[apparent magnitude]] of Mars is +0.71 with a standard deviation of 1.05. Because the orbit of Mars is eccentric, the magnitude at [[opposition (planets)|opposition]] from the Sun can range from about −3.0 to −1.4. The minimum brightness is magnitude +1.86 when the planet is near [[Apsis|aphelion]] and in [[conjunction (astronomy)|conjunction]] with the Sun. At its brightest, Mars (along with [[Jupiter]]) is second only to Venus in apparent brightness. Mars usually appears distinctly yellow, orange, or red. When farthest away from Earth, it is more than seven times farther away than when it is closest. Mars is usually close enough for particularly good viewing once or twice at 15-year or 17-year intervals.{{cite web |title=Mars Close Approach |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/night-sky/close-approach |access-date=18 January 2022 |website=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |date=10 November 2017 |archive-date=8 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108232313/https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/night-sky/close-approach/ |url-status=live}} Optical ground-based telescopes are typically limited to resolving features about {{convert|300|km}} across when Earth and Mars are closest because of Earth's atmosphere.{{cite web |title=Slide 2 Earth Telescope View of Mars |url=http://www.lpi.usra.edu/publications/slidesets/redplanet2/slide_2.html |work=The Red Planet: A Survey of Mars |publisher=Lunar and Planetary Institute |access-date=28 November 2011 |archive-date=18 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518203239/https://www.lpi.usra.edu/publications/slidesets/redplanet2/slide_2.html |url-status=live}} As Mars approaches opposition, it begins a period of [[Apparent retrograde motion|retrograde motion]], which means it will appear to move backwards in a looping curve with respect to the background stars. This retrograde motion lasts for about 72 days, and Mars reaches its peak apparent brightness in the middle of this interval. == Moons == {{Main|Moons of Mars|Phobos (moon)|Deimos (moon)}} [[File:PIA17351-ApparentSizes-MarsDeimosPhobos-EarthMoon.jpg|thumb|The moons of Mars [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]] and [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]] as seen from Mars, compared at [[angular size|apparent size]] to the in apparent and actual size much larger [[Moon]] as seen from Earth. If they would be as far away from Mars as the Moon from Earth, they would appear as faint star-like features in the Martian sky.]] [[File:Phobos fly-by animation ESA223006.gif|thumb|Orbits of natural and artificial satellites around Mars at scale, with the furthest (Deimos) at {{convert|23,460|km|mi|abbr=on}}]] Mars has two relatively small (compared to Earth's) natural moons, [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]] (about {{convert|22|km|abbr=on}} in diameter) and [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]] (about {{convert|12|km|abbr=on}} in diameter), which orbit at {{convert|9376|km|mi|abbr=on}} and {{convert|23,460|km|mi|abbr=on}} around the planet. The origin of both moons is unclear, although a popular theory states that they were asteroids captured into Martian orbit. Both satellites were discovered in 1877 by [[Asaph Hall]] and were named after the characters [[Phobos (mythology)|Phobos]] (the deity of panic and fear) and [[Deimos (mythology)|Deimos]] (the deity of terror and dread), twins from [[Greek mythology]] who accompanied their father [[Ares]], god of war, into battle.{{Cite web |title=Planetary Names |url=https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/Planets#MartianSystem |access-date=30 May 2022 |website=planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov |archive-date=30 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231230164721/https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/Planets#MartianSystem |url-status=live}} [[Mars (mythology)|Mars]] was the Roman equivalent to Ares. In modern [[Greek language|Greek]], the planet retains its ancient name ''Ares'' (Aris: ''Άρης''). From the surface of Mars, the motions of Phobos and Deimos appear different from that of the Earth's satellite, the [[Moon]]. Phobos rises in the west, sets in the east, and rises again in just 11 hours. Deimos, being only just outside [[synchronous orbit]]{{Snd}}where the orbital period would match the planet's period of rotation{{Snd}}rises as expected in the east, but slowly. Because the orbit of Phobos is below a synchronous altitude, [[tidal force]]s from Mars are gradually lowering its orbit. In about 50 million years, it could either crash into Mars's surface or break up into a ring structure around the planet.{{cite web |title=Phobos |url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/mars-moons/phobos/in-depth |access-date=12 January 2022 |date=19 December 2019 |website=NASA Solar System Exploration |archive-date=12 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220112004526/https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/mars-moons/phobos/in-depth/ |url-status=live}} The origin of the two satellites is not well understood. Their low albedo and [[carbonaceous chondrite]] composition have been regarded as similar to asteroids, supporting a capture theory. The unstable orbit of Phobos would seem to point toward a relatively recent capture. But both have [[circular orbit]]s near the equator, which is unusual for captured objects, and the required capture dynamics are complex. Accretion early in the history of Mars is plausible, but would not account for a composition resembling asteroids rather than Mars itself, if that is confirmed.{{cite web |title=Explaining the Birth of the Martian Moons |date=23 September 2016 |url=https://aasnova.org/2016/09/23/explaining-the-birth-of-the-martian-moons/ |access-date=13 December 2021 |language=en-US |website=AAS Nova |publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]] |archive-date=13 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211213022350/https://aasnova.org/2016/09/23/explaining-the-birth-of-the-martian-moons/ |url-status=live}} Mars may have yet-undiscovered moons, smaller than {{convert|50|to|100|m}} in diameter, and a dust ring is predicted to exist between Phobos and Deimos.{{cite conference |last1=Adler |first1=M. |last2=Owen |first2=W. |last3=Riedel |first3=J. |date=June 2012 |title=Use of MRO Optical Navigation Camera to Prepare for Mars Sample Return |url=http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/marsconcepts2012/pdf/4337.pdf |conference=Concepts and Approaches for Mars Exploration. 12–14 June 2012. Houston, Texas. |issue=1679 |at=4337 |bibcode=2012LPICo1679.4337A |access-date=28 August 2012 |archive-date=26 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226060810/https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/marsconcepts2012/pdf/4337.pdf%20 |url-status=live}} A third possibility for their origin as satellites of Mars is the involvement of a third body or a type of impact disruption. More-recent lines of evidence for Phobos having a highly porous interior, and suggesting a composition containing mainly [[phyllosilicates]] and other minerals known from Mars, point toward an origin of Phobos from material ejected by an impact on Mars that reaccreted in Martian orbit, similar to the [[Giant impact hypothesis|prevailing theory]] for the origin of Earth's satellite. Although the [[visible and near-infrared]] (VNIR) spectra of the moons of Mars resemble those of outer-belt asteroids, the [[thermal infrared]] spectra of Phobos are reported to be inconsistent with [[chondrite]]s of any class. It is also possible that Phobos and Deimos were fragments of an older moon, formed by debris from a large impact on Mars, and then destroyed by a more recent impact upon the satellite.{{cite journal |title=Dynamical evidence for Phobos and Deimos as remnants of a disrupted common progenitor |doi=10.1038/s41550-021-01306-2 |journal=Nature Astronomy |date=22 February 2021 |volume=5 |pages=539–543 |first1=Amirhossein |last1=Bagheri |first2=Amir |last2=Khan |first3=Michael |last3=Efroimsky |first4=Mikhail |last4=Kruglyakov |first5=Domenico |last5=Giardini |issue=6 |bibcode=2021NatAs...5..539B |s2cid=233924981}} More recently, a study conducted by a team of researchers from multiple countries suggests that a lost moon, at least fifteen times the size of Phobos, may have existed in the past. By analyzing rocks which point to tidal processes on the planet, it is possible that these tides may have been regulated by a past moon.{{Cite web |last=Benningfield |first=Damond |date=11 December 2025 |title=Ancient Lake on Mars May Have Risen and Fallen Under the Tidal Pull of a Long Lost Moon |url=https://www.zmescience.com/space/ancient-lake-on-mars-may-have-risen-and-fallen-under-the-tidal-pull-of-a-long-lost-moon/ |access-date=13 December 2025 |website=ZME Science |language=en-US}} == Human observations and exploration == {{Main|Exploration of Mars|History of Mars observation}} The history of observations of Mars is marked by oppositions of Mars when the planet is closest to Earth and hence is most easily visible, which occur every couple of years. Even more notable are the [[perihelic opposition]]s of Mars, which are distinguished because Mars is close to perihelion, making it even closer to Earth. === Ancient observations === The ancient [[Sumer]]ians named Mars [[Nergal]], the god of war and plague. During Sumerian times, Nergal was a minor deity of little significance, but, during later times, his main cult center was the city of [[Nineveh]].{{cite book |last1=Rabkin |first1=Eric S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a2QP30zybNkC&pg=PA11 |title=Mars: A Tour of the Human Imagination |date=2005 |publisher=Praeger |isbn=978-0-275-98719-0 |location=Westport, Connecticut |pages=9–11}} In Mesopotamian texts, Mars is referred to as the "star of judgement of the fate of the dead".{{cite book |last1=Thompson |first1=Henry O. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kc0UAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA125 |title=Mekal: The God of Beth-Shan |date=1970 |publisher=E. J. Brill |location=Leiden |page=125}} The existence of Mars as a wandering object in the night sky was also recorded by the ancient [[Egyptian astronomy|Egyptian astronomers]] and, by 1534 BCE, they were familiar with the [[Apparent retrograde motion|retrograde motion]] of the planet. By the period of the [[Neo-Babylonian Empire]], the [[Babylonian astronomy|Babylonian astronomers]] were making regular records of the positions of the planets and systematic observations of their behavior. For Mars, they knew that the planet made 37 [[Orbital period|synodic periods]], or 42 circuits of the zodiac, every 79 years. They invented arithmetic methods for making minor corrections to the predicted positions of the planets. In [[Ancient Greece]], the planet was known as {{langx|grc|[[Pyroeis|Πυρόεις]]|label=none}}.{{cite book |last=Cicero |first=Marcus Tullius |url=https://archive.org/details/marcitulliicicer00cice |title=De Natura Deorum |publisher=Methuen |year=1896 |location=London |translator=Francis Brooks |trans-title=On the Nature of the Gods}} Commonly, the Greek name for the planet now referred to as Mars, was Ares. It was the Romans who named the planet Mars, for their god of war, often represented by the sword and shield of the planet's namesake.{{Cite web |last=NASA |date=9 October 2022 |title=All About Mars |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/allaboutmars/mystique/history/early/ |website=mars.nasa.gov |access-date=10 October 2022 |archive-date=10 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221010032729/https://mars.nasa.gov/allaboutmars/mystique/history/early/ |url-status=live}} In the fourth century BCE, [[Aristotle]] noted that Mars disappeared behind the Moon during an [[occultation]], indicating that the planet was farther away.{{Cite journal |last=Stephenson |first=F. Richard |date=November 2000 |title=A Lunar Occultation of Mars Observed by Aristotle |journal=Journal for the History of Astronomy |volume=31 |issue=4 |pages=342–344 |bibcode=2000JHA....31..342S |doi=10.1177/002182860003100405 |issn=0021-8286 |s2cid=125518456 }} [[Ptolemy]], a Greek living in [[Alexandria]], attempted to address the problem of the orbital motion of Mars. Ptolemy's model and his collective work on astronomy was presented in the multi-volume collection later called the ''[[Almagest]]'' (from the Arabic for "greatest"), which became the authoritative treatise on [[Medieval astronomy|Western astronomy]] for the next fourteen centuries.{{citation |last=McCluskey |first=S. C. |title=Astronomies and Cultures in Early Medieval Europe |pages=20–21 |year=1998 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-77852-7}} Literature from ancient China confirms that Mars was known by [[Chinese astronomy|Chinese astronomers]] by no later than the fourth century BCE. In the [[East Asian]] cultures, Mars is traditionally referred to as the "fire star" ({{lang|zh|火星}}) based on the [[Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)|''Wuxing'' system]].{{cite book |last=de Groot |first=Jan Jakob Maria |title=Religion in China – Universism: A Key to the Study of Taoism and Confucianism |date=1912 |publisher=G. P. Putnam's Sons |series=American Lectures on the History of Religions, volume 10 |page=300 |chapter=Fung Shui |oclc=491180 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZAaP7dyjCrAC&pg=PA300 |access-date=5 January 2016}}{{cite book |last=Crump |first=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mk3vxD3Ib_sC&pg=PT43 |title=The Japanese Numbers Game: The Use and Understanding of Numbers in Modern Japan |date=1992 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-05609-0 |series=Nissan Institute/Routledge Japanese Studies Series |pages=39–40}}{{cite book |last=Hulbert |first=Homer Bezaleel |url=https://archive.org/details/passingkorea01hulbgoog |title=The Passing of Korea |date=1909 |publisher=Doubleday, Page & Company |page=[https://archive.org/details/passingkorea01hulbgoog/page/n538 426] |oclc=26986808 |orig-year=1906}} === Early modern observations === [[File:Kepler Mars retrograde.jpg|thumb|upright=.9|Diagram of the [[geocentric]] trajectory of Mars through several periods of [[apparent retrograde motion]] in [[Johannes Kepler]]'s ''Astronomia Nova'' (1609)]] In 1609 [[Johannes Kepler]] published a 10-year study of Martian orbit,{{cite web | last=Cooper | first=Keith | title=Johannes Kepler: Unlocking the Secrets of Planetary Motion | website=Space | date=22 December 2023 | url=https://www.space.com/15787-johannes-kepler.html | access-date=16 April 2025}} using the [[diurnal parallax]] of Mars, measured by [[Tycho Brahe]], to make a preliminary calculation of the relative distance to the planet. From Brahe's observations of Mars, Kepler deduced that the planet orbited the Sun not in a circle, but in an [[ellipse]]. Moreover, Kepler showed that Mars sped up as it approached the Sun and slowed down as it moved farther away, in a manner that later physicists would explain as a consequence of the [[conservation of angular momentum]].{{Cite book |last1=Frautschi |first1=Steven C. |title=The Mechanical Universe: Mechanics and Heat |title-link=The Mechanical Universe |last2=Olenick |first2=Richard P. |last3=Apostol |first3=Tom M. |last4=Goodstein |first4=David L. |date=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-71590-4 |edition=Advanced |location=Cambridge [Cambridgeshire] |oclc=227002144 |author-link=Steven Frautschi |author-link3=Tom M. Apostol |author-link4=David L. Goodstein}}{{Rp|pages=433–437}} [[File:Lowell - Mars (1894) - Huyghens' drawing of the Syrtis Major, Nov. 28, 1659.jpg|thumb|First drawn record of Martian features (Manuscript K), by [[Christiaan Huygens]], observed on 28 November 1659.{{cite web | last=Huygens | first=Christiaan | title=I. (Manuscrit K). 1657-1659., Oeuvres complètes. Tome XV. Observations astronomiques, Christiaan Huygens | publisher=DBNL | url=https://www.dbnl.org/tekst/huyg003oeuv15_01/huyg003oeuv15_01_0002.php | language=nl | access-date=15 April 2025}} The feature is probably [[Syrtis Major Planum]]. Huygens calculated from the moving of the features the rotation of Mars.]] In 1610 the first use of a telescope for astronomical observation, including Mars, was performed by Italian astronomer [[Galileo Galilei]]. With the telescope the diurnal parallax of Mars was again measured in an effort to determine the Sun-Earth distance. This was first performed by [[Giovanni Domenico Cassini]] in 1672. The early parallax measurements were hampered by the quality of the instruments. The only [[occultation]] of Mars by Venus observed was that of 13 October 1590, seen by [[Michael Maestlin]] at [[Heidelberg]]. === Martian "canals" === {{Main|Martian canals}} [[File:Mars_-_MEC-1_Prototype._LOC_2013593160.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|A 1962 map of Mars published by the U.S. [[Aeronautical Chart and Information Center]], showing canals snaking through the Martian landscape. At the time, the existence of canals was still highly controversial as no close-up pictures of Mars had been taken (until [[Mariner 4]]'s flyby in 1965).]] By the 19th century, the resolution of telescopes reached a level sufficient for surface features to be identified. On 5 September 1877, a perihelic opposition to Mars occurred. The Italian astronomer [[Giovanni Schiaparelli]] used a {{convert|22|cm|adj=on}} telescope in [[Milan]] to help produce the first detailed map of Mars. These maps notably contained features he called ''canali'', which, with the possible exception of the natural canyon [[Valles Marineris]], were later shown to be an [[optical illusion]]. These ''canali'' were supposedly long, straight lines on the surface of Mars, to which he gave names of famous rivers on Earth. His term, which means "channels" or "grooves", was popularly mistranslated in English as "canals".{{cite web |last=Milner |first=Richard |date=6 October 2011 |title=Tracing the Canals of Mars: An Astronomer's Obsession |url=https://www.space.com/13197-mars-canals-water-history-lowell.html |access-date=25 December 2021 |website=Space.com |archive-date=25 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225043755/https://www.space.com/13197-mars-canals-water-history-lowell.html |url-status=live}} Influenced by the observations, the orientalist [[Percival Lowell]] founded [[Lowell Observatory|an observatory]] which had 30- and 45-centimetre (12- and 18-in) telescopes. The observatory was used for the exploration of Mars during the last good opportunity in 1894, and the following less favorable oppositions. He published several books on Mars and life on the planet, which had a great influence on the public.{{cite news |last=Dunlap |first=David W. |date=1 October 2015 |title=Life on Mars? You Read It Here First. |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/30/insider/life-on-mars-you-read-it-here-first.html |access-date=1 October 2015 |archive-date=2 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002192143/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/30/insider/life-on-mars-you-read-it-here-first.html |url-status=live}} The ''canali'' were independently observed by other astronomers, such as [[Henri Joseph Perrotin]] and [[Louis Thollon]] in Nice, using one of the largest telescopes of that time. The seasonal changes (consisting of the diminishing of the polar caps and the dark areas formed during Martian summers) in combination with the canals led to speculation about life on Mars, and it was a long-held belief that Mars contained vast seas and vegetation. As bigger telescopes were used, fewer long, straight ''canali'' were observed. During observations in 1909 by [[Antoniadi]] with an {{convert|84|cm|adj=on}} telescope, irregular patterns were observed, but no ''canali'' were seen. === First exploration === [[File:M04 12.jpg|thumb|The very first two images from, and of, another planet (Mars), by [[Mariner 4]],{{cite web | title=Attempt to Take Pictures of Black Space Scrubbed | website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) | date=21 August 1965 | url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/attempt-to-take-pictures-of-black-space-scrubbed/ | access-date=15 April 2025}} the second spacecraft to reach Mars and the first to transmit data (15 July 1965). The data disproved Mars being hospitable and having canals.]] The first spacecraft from Earth to visit Mars was [[Mars 1]] of the [[Soviet space program|Soviet Union]], which flew by in 1963, but contact was lost en route. [[NASA]]'s ''[[Mariner 4]]'' followed and became the first spacecraft to successfully transmit from Mars; launched on 28 November 1964, it made its closest approach to the planet on 15 July 1965. ''Mariner 4'' detected the weak Martian radiation belt, measured at about 0.1% that of Earth, and captured the first images of another planet from deep space.{{cite web |date=20 December 2017 |title=Mariner 04 |url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/mariner-04/in-depth |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803192306/https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/mariner-04/in-depth/ |archive-date=3 August 2020 |access-date=9 February 2020 |website=NASA Solar System Exploration |quote=The Mariner 4 mission, the second of two Mars flyby attempts launched in 1964 by NASA, was one of the great early successes of the agency, and indeed the Space Age, returning the very first photos of another planet from deep space.}} {{PD-notice}} {{cite web |title=Spacecraft – Details – Mariner 4 |url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1964-077A |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180904174225/https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraftDisplay.do?id=1964-077A |archive-date=4 September 2018 |access-date=9 February 2020 |website=NASA – NSSDCA |quote=Mariner 4...represented the first successful flyby of the planet Mars, returning the first pictures of the martian surface. These represented the first images of another planet ever returned from deep space.}} {{PD-notice}} Once [[spacecraft]] visited the planet during the 1960s and 1970s, many previous concepts of Mars were radically broken. After the results of the ''Viking'' life-detection experiments, the hypothesis of a dead planet was generally accepted. The data from ''Mariner 9'' and ''Viking'' allowed better maps of Mars to be made. ===Renewed exploration=== Until 1997 and after Viking 1 shut down in 1982, Mars was only visited by three unsuccessful probes, two flying past without contact ([[Phobos 1]], 1988; [[Mars Observer]], 1993), and one ([[Phobos 2]] 1989) malfunctioning in orbit before reaching its destination [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]]. In 1997 [[Mars Pathfinder]] became the first successful rover mission beyond the Moon and started together with ''[[Mars Global Surveyor]]'' (operated until late 2006) an uninterrupted active robotic presence at Mars that has lasted until today. It produced complete, extremely detailed maps of the Martian topography, magnetic field and surface minerals. Starting with these missions a range of new improved crewless [[spacecraft]], including [[orbiter]]s, [[Mars lander|landers]], and [[Mars rover|rovers]], have been sent to Mars, with successful missions by the NASA (United States), [[Jaxa]] ([[Japan]]), [[ESA]], [[United Kingdom]], [[ISRO]] ([[India]]), [[Roscosmos]] (Russia), the [[Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre|United Arab Emirates]], and [[CNSA]] ([[China]]) to study the planet's surface, climate, and geology,{{cite web |date=29 July 2020 |title=Why we explore Mars—and what decades of missions have revealed |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/mars-exploration-article |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210218212120/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/mars-exploration-article |url-status=dead |archive-date=18 February 2021 |access-date=7 December 2021 |website=National Geographic |first=Nadia |last=Drake |author-link=Nadia Drake |language=en}} uncovering the different elements of the history and dynamic of the hydrosphere of Mars and possible traces of ancient life. NASA provides two online tools: Mars Trek, which provides visualizations of the planet using data from 50 years of exploration, and [[Experience Curiosity]], which simulates traveling on Mars in 3-D with ''Curiosity''.{{cite web |title=New Online Tools Bring NASA's Journey to Mars to a New Generation |url=http://www.nasa.gov/press-release/new-online-tools-bring-nasa-s-journey-to-mars-to-new-generation-of-explorers |access-date=5 August 2015 |date=5 August 2015 |website=NASA |archive-date=7 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150807234318/http://www.nasa.gov/press-release/new-online-tools-bring-nasa-s-journey-to-mars-to-new-generation-of-explorers/ |url-status=dead}}{{cite magazine |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/nasa-mars-trek |title=Explore the Red Planet with Nasa's Mars Trek |magazine=Wired UK |date=10 July 2015 |access-date=31 March 2022 |first=Daniel |last=Culpan |archive-date=31 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220331183510/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/nasa-mars-trek |url-status=live}} ===Future=== Planned missions to Mars include: * NASA's [[EscaPADE]] spacecraft, launched on 13 November 2025.{{Cite tweet |number=1827079568470995106 |user=blueorigin |title=#NewGlenn's inaugural mission aims to send @NASA's ESCAPADE to Mars, with a launch date no earlier than October 13.}}{{cite web |url=https://www.blueorigin.com/missions/ng-2 |title=New Glenn Mission NG-2 |publisher=Blue Origin |access-date=14 November 2025 |archive-date=13 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251113025923/https://www.blueorigin.com/missions/ng-2 |url-status=dead }}{{Cite tweet |number= 1989074636055998558 |user=blueorigin |title= LIFTOFF! Key areas include establishing telecommunications, payload delivery and surface imaging.{{Cite web |title=NASA Selects Commercial Service Studies to Enable Mars Robotic Science |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-selects-commercial-service-studies-to-enable-mars-robotic-science |access-date=1 May 2024 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |language=en-US}} In 2025, an ad hoc committee was convened by the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine]] (NASEM) to prioritize science objectives to guide human exploration on Mars.{{Cite Q|https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q139854992}} Out of hundreds of possible projects, the four panels of the committee (Astrobiology, Geosciences, Atmospheric Science and Space Physics, and Biological and Physical Sciences and Human Factors) highlighted eleven as the top science objectives to pursue, with the top priority being searching for current or extinct indigenous life on Mars. == Habitability and habitation == {{Main|1 = Life on Mars}} [[File:41586 2025 9413 Fig3 HTML.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Layering, nodules, reaction fronts and organic detections marked in an image from ancient fossilized mud at [[Cheyava Falls]], being the most promising finds potentially showing traces of remains of ancient Martian life.]] During the late 19th century, it was widely accepted in the astronomical community that Mars had life-supporting qualities, including the presence of oxygen and water. However, in 1894 [[William Wallace Campbell|W. W. Campbell]] at [[Lick Observatory]] observed the planet and found that "if water vapor or oxygen occur in the atmosphere of Mars it is in quantities too small to have been detected by spectroscopes then available". That observation contradicted many of the measurements of the time and was not widely accepted. Campbell and [[Vesto Slipher|V. M. Slipher]] repeated the study in 1909 using better instruments, but with the same results. It was not until the findings were confirmed by [[Walter Sydney Adams|W. S. Adams]] in 1925 that the myth of the Earth-like habitability of Mars was finally broken. However, even in the 1960s, articles were published on Martian biology, putting aside explanations other than life for the seasonal changes on Mars. The current understanding of [[planetary habitability]]{{Snd}}the ability of a world to develop environmental conditions favorable to the emergence of life{{Snd}}favors planets that have liquid water on their surface. Most often this requires the orbit of a planet to lie within the [[circumstellar habitable zone|habitable zone]], which for the Sun is estimated to extend from within the orbit of Earth to about that of Mars.{{cite journal |last1=Kopparapu |first1=Ravi Kumar |last2=Ramirez |first2=Ramses |last3=Kasting |first3=James F. |last4=Eymet |first4=Vincent |last5=Robinson |first5=Tyler D. |last6=Mahadevan |first6=Suvrath |last7=Terrien |first7=Ryan C. |last8=Domagal-Goldman |first8=Shawn |last9=Meadows |first9=Victoria |last10=Deshpande |first10=Rohit |date=2013 |title=Habitable Zones Around Main-Sequence Stars: New Estimates |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=765 |issue=2 |pages=131 |arxiv=1301.6674 |bibcode=2013ApJ...765..131K |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/765/2/131 |s2cid=76651902}} During perihelion, Mars dips inside this region, but Mars's thin (low-pressure) atmosphere prevents liquid water from existing over large regions for extended periods. The past flow of liquid water demonstrates the planet's potential for habitability. Recent evidence has suggested that any water on the Martian surface may have been too salty and acidic to support regular terrestrial life. The environmental conditions on Mars are a challenge to sustaining organic life: the planet has little [[heat transfer]] across its surface, it has poor insulation against [[Solar wind#Atmospheres|bombardment]] by the [[solar wind]] due to the absence of a magnetosphere and has insufficient atmospheric pressure to retain water in a liquid form (water instead [[Sublimation (phase transition)|sublimes]] to a gaseous state). Mars is nearly, or perhaps totally, geologically dead; the end of volcanic activity has apparently stopped the recycling of chemicals and minerals between the surface and interior of the planet. Evidence suggests that the planet was once significantly more habitable than it is today, but whether living [[organism]]s ever existed there remains unknown. The [[Viking probes|''Viking'' probes]] of the mid-1970s carried experiments designed to detect microorganisms in Martian soil at their respective landing sites and had positive results, including a temporary increase in {{chem2|CO2}} production on exposure to water and nutrients. This sign of life was later disputed by scientists, resulting in a continuing debate, with NASA scientist [[Gilbert Levin]] asserting that ''Viking'' may have found life.{{cite web |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=4 August 2021 |title=Gilbert V. Levin, Who Said He Found Signs of Life on Mars, Dies at 97 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/04/science/space/gilbert-v-levin-dead.html |access-date=4 August 2021 |work=The New York Times |archive-date=4 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210804185707/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/04/science/space/gilbert-v-levin-dead.html |url-status=live}} A 2014 analysis of Martian meteorite EETA79001 found [[chlorate]], [[perchlorate]], and [[nitrate]] ions in sufficiently high concentrations to suggest that they are widespread on Mars. UV and X-ray radiation would turn chlorate and perchlorate ions into other, highly [[redox|reactive]] [[Oxyanion|oxychlorines]], indicating that any organic molecules would have to be buried under the surface to survive.{{cite journal |last1=Kounaves |first1=S. P. |year=2014 |title=Evidence of martian perchlorate, chlorate, and nitrate in Mars meteorite EETA79001: implications for oxidants and organics |journal=Icarus |volume=229 |pages=206–213 |bibcode=2014Icar..229..206K |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2013.11.012}} Small quantities of [[methane]] and [[formaldehyde]] detected by Mars orbiters are both claimed to be possible evidence for life, as these [[chemical compound]]s would quickly break down in the Martian atmosphere. Alternatively, these compounds may instead be replenished by volcanic or other geological means, such as [[serpentinite]]. [[Impactite|Impact glass]], formed by the impact of meteors, which on Earth can preserve signs of life, has also been found on the surface of the impact craters on Mars.{{cite news |last=Nickel |first=Mark |date=18 April 2014 |title=Impact glass stores biodata for millions of years |publisher=Brown University |url=https://news.brown.edu/articles/2014/04/impactglass |access-date=9 June 2015 |archive-date=17 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150617122630/https://news.brown.edu/articles/2014/04/impactglass |url-status=live}}{{cite journal |last1=Schultz |first1=P. H. |last2=Harris |first2=R. Scott |last3=Clemett |first3=S. J. |last4=Thomas-Keprta |first4=K. L. |last5=Zárate |first5=M. |date=June 2014 |title=Preserved flora and organics in impact melt breccias |journal=[[Geology (journal)|Geology]] |volume=42 |issue=6 |pages=515–518 |bibcode=2014Geo....42..515S |doi=10.1130/G35343.1 |s2cid=39019154 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2060/20140013110}} Likewise, the glass in impact craters on Mars could have preserved signs of life, if life existed at the site.{{cite press release |url=http://www.nasa.gov/press-release/nasa-spacecraft-detects-impact-glass-on-surface-of-mars |title=NASA Spacecraft Detects Impact Glass on Surface of Mars |publisher=NASA |first1=Dwayne |last1=Brown |first2=Guy |last2=Webster |first3=Kevin |last3=Stacey |date=8 June 2015 |access-date=9 June 2015 |archive-date=9 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150609132637/http://www.nasa.gov/press-release/nasa-spacecraft-detects-impact-glass-on-surface-of-mars/ |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}{{cite news |last=Stacey |first=Kevin |date=8 June 2015 |title=Martian glass: Window into possible past life? |publisher=Brown University |url=https://news.brown.edu/articles/2015/06/marsglass |access-date=9 June 2015 |archive-date=11 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150611003248/http://news.brown.edu/articles/2015/06/marsglass |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last=Temming |first=Maria |date=12 June 2015 |title=Exotic Glass Could Help Unravel Mysteries of Mars |work=Scientific American |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/exotic-glass-could-help-unravel-mysteries-of-mars/ |access-date=15 June 2015 |archive-date=15 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150615010829/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/exotic-glass-could-help-unravel-mysteries-of-mars/ |url-status=live}} The [[Cheyava Falls]] rock discovered on Mars in June 2024 has been designated by NASA as a "potential [[biosignature]]" and was core sampled by the [[Perseverance (rover)|Perseverance]] rover for possible return to Earth and further examination. Although highly intriguing, no definitive final determination on a biological or abiotic origin of this rock can be made with the data currently available.{{Cite web |title=NASA Says Mars Rover Discovered Potential Biosignature Last Year - NASA |work=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-says-mars-rover-discovered-potential-biosignature-last-year/ |access-date=10 September 2025 |language=en-US}} === Human mission proposals === [[File:NextSTEP_mars-soil-excavation.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|A NASA [[ISRU]] system concept for autonomous robotic excavation and processing of Mars soil to extract water for use in exploration missions.]] Several plans for a [[human mission to Mars]] have been proposed, but none have come to fruition. |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=2–11 |bibcode=2018NewSp...6....2M |doi=10.1089/space.2018.29013.emu |issn=2168-0256 |access-date=27 August 2022 |archive-date=29 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190629143329/https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/space.2018.29013.emu |url-status=live}} As of 2024, SpaceX has proceeded with the development of the [[SpaceX Starship|Starship]] launch vehicle with the goal of Mars colonization. In plans shared with the company in April 2024, Elon Musk envisions the beginning of a Mars colony within the next twenty years. This would be enabled by the planned [[mass manufacturing]] of Starship and initially sustained by resupply from Earth, and [[in situ resource utilization]] on Mars, until the Mars colony reaches full self sustainability.{{Cite web |author1=Howell |first=Elizabeth |date=13 April 2024 |title=SpaceX's giant Starship will be 500 feet tall for Mars missions, Elon Musk says (video) |url=https://www.space.com/spacex-starship-500-feet-tall-mars-missions-elon-musk |access-date=20 April 2024 |website=Space.com |language=en}} Any future human mission to Mars will likely take place within [[Exploration of Mars#Launch windows|the optimal Mars launch window]], which occurs every 26 months. The moon Phobos has been proposed as an anchor point for a [[space elevator]].{{Cite journal |last=Weinstein |first=Leonard M. |date=2003 |title=Space Colonization Using Space-Elevators from Phobos |url=https://space.nss.org/wp-content/uploads/2003-Space-Colonization-Using-Space-Elevators-From-Phobos.pdf |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |location=Albuquerque, New Mexico (USA) |publisher=AIP |volume=654 |pages=1227–1235 |bibcode=2003AIPC..654.1227W |doi=10.1063/1.1541423 |s2cid=1661518 |hdl=2060/20030065879 |access-date=6 December 2022 |archive-date=19 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230119073347/https://space.nss.org/wp-content/uploads/2003-Space-Colonization-Using-Space-Elevators-From-Phobos.pdf |url-status=live}} Besides national space agencies and space companies, groups such as the [[Mars Society]]{{Cite news |last=Bichell |first=Rae Ellen |date=6 July 2017 |title=To Prepare For Mars Settlement, Simulated Missions Explore Utah's Desert |url=https://www.npr.org/2017/07/06/522060920/to-prepare-for-mars-settlement-simulated-missions-explore-utahs-desert |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221231181009/https://www.npr.org/2017/07/06/522060920/to-prepare-for-mars-settlement-simulated-missions-explore-utahs-desert |archive-date=31 December 2022 |access-date=31 December 2022 |work=[[NPR]] |language=en}} and [[The Planetary Society]]{{Cite web |last=Boyle |first=Alan |date=29 September 2015 |title=Destination Phobos: 'Humans Orbiting Mars' report goes public |url=https://www.geekwire.com/2015/destination-phobos-humans-orbiting-mars-report-goes-public/ |website=GeekWire}} advocate for human missions to Mars. == In culture == {{Main|Mars in culture|Mars in fiction}} {{see also|Planets in astrology#Mars}} [[File:The War of the Worlds by Henrique Alvim Corrêa, original graphic 15.jpg|thumb|''[[The War of the Worlds]]'' by [[H. G. Wells]], 1897, depicts an [[Alien invasion|invasion of Earth]] by fictional Martians.]] Mars is named after the [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] [[Mars (mythology)|god of war]] ([[Greek mythology|Greek]] [[Ares]]), but was also associated with the demi-god [[Heracles]] (Roman [[Hercules]]) by ancient Greek astronomers, as detailed by [[Aristotle]].[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0063%3Aalphabetic+letter%3DP%3Aentry+group%3D4%3Aentry%3Dplanetae-cn "Planetae"], in ''Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities'', pp. 922, 923. This association between Mars and war dates back at least to [[Babylonian astronomy]], in which the planet was named for the god [[Nergal]], deity of war and destruction.{{Cite book |last=Koch |first=Ulla Susanne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8QiwAqGlmAQC |title=Mesopotamian Astrology: An Introduction to Babylonian and Assyrian Celestial Divination |date=1995 |publisher=Museum Tusculanum Press |isbn=978-87-7289-287-0 |pages=128–129 |language=en}}{{Cite journal |last=Cecilia |first=Ludovica |date=6 November 2019 |title=A Late Composition Dedicated to Nergal |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/aofo-2019-0014/html |journal=Altorientalische Forschungen |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=204–213 |doi=10.1515/aofo-2019-0014 |hdl=1871.1/f23ff882-1539-4906-bc08-049906f8d505 |s2cid=208269607 |issn=2196-6761 |hdl-access=free |access-date=22 March 2022 |archive-date=22 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220322014922/https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/aofo-2019-0014/html |url-status=live}} It persisted into modern times, as exemplified by [[Gustav Holst]]'s orchestral suite ''[[The Planets]]'', whose famous first movement labels Mars "The Bringer of War".{{Cite journal |last=Reid |first=James |date=2011 |title=An Astronomer's Guide to Holst's ''The Planets'' |url=https://skyandtelescope.org/wp-content/uploads/Reid_on_Holst.pdf |journal=Sky and Telescope |volume=121 |issue=1 |pages=66 |bibcode=2011S&T...121a..66R |access-date=22 March 2022 |archive-date=22 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220322014920/https://skyandtelescope.org/wp-content/uploads/Reid_on_Holst.pdf |url-status=live}} [[Planet symbols|The planet's symbol]], a circle with a spear pointing out to the upper right, is also used as a symbol for the male gender.{{cite web |title=Solar System Symbols |url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/resources/680/solar-system-symbols |access-date=7 December 2021 |website=NASA Solar System Exploration |date=30 January 2018 |archive-date=20 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211220171351/https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/resources/680/solar-system-symbols/ |url-status=live}} The symbol dates from at least the 11th century, though a possible predecessor has been found in the Greek [[Oxyrhynchus Papyri]]. {{cite book |title=Astronomical papyri from Oxyrhynchus |last=Jones |first=Alexander |date=1999 |pages=62–63 |publisher=American Philosophical Society |isbn=978-0-87169-233-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8MokzymQ43IC}} [[File:Holst - The Planets - Mars, The Bringer of War (TMO Orchestra, Incheon, 2023).opus|thumb|The first movement of Gustav Holst's The Planets - Mars, The Bringer of War (TMO Orchestra, Incheon, 2023)]] The idea that Mars was populated by intelligent [[Martian]]s became widespread in the late 19th century. [[Giovanni Schiaparelli|Schiaparelli's]] "canali" observations combined with [[Percival Lowell]]'s books on the subject put forward the standard notion of a planet that was a drying, cooling, dying world with ancient civilizations constructing irrigation works.{{cite web |last1=Eschner |first1=Kat |title=The Bizarre Beliefs of Astronomer Percival Lowell |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/bizarre-beliefs-astronomer-percival-lowell-180962432/ |access-date=25 December 2021 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en |archive-date=25 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225111323/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/bizarre-beliefs-astronomer-percival-lowell-180962432/ |url-status=live}} Many other observations and proclamations by notable personalities added to what has been termed "Mars Fever". In the present day, high-resolution mapping of the surface of Mars has revealed no artifacts of habitation, but pseudoscientific speculation about intelligent life on Mars still continues. Reminiscent of the ''canali'' observations, these speculations are based on small scale features perceived in the spacecraft images, such as "pyramids" and the "[[Cydonia (Mars)|Face on Mars]]".{{Cite book |last=Plait |first=Philip C. |title=Bad Astronomy: Misconceptions and Misuses Revealed, from Astrology to the Moon Landing 'Hoax' |title-link=Bad Astronomy |date=2002 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=0-471-40976-6 |location=New York |pages=233–234 |oclc=48885221 |author-link=Phil Plait}} In his book ''[[Cosmos (Sagan book)|Cosmos]]'', planetary astronomer [[Carl Sagan]] wrote: "Mars has become a kind of mythic arena onto which we have projected our Earthly hopes and fears." The depiction of Mars in fiction has been stimulated by its dramatic red color and by nineteenth-century scientific speculations that its surface conditions might support not just life but intelligent life. This gave way to many [[science fiction]] stories involving these concepts, such as [[H. G. Wells]]'s ''[[The War of the Worlds]]'', in which Martians seek to escape their dying planet by invading Earth; [[Ray Bradbury]]'s ''[[The Martian Chronicles]]'', in which human explorers accidentally destroy a Martian civilization; as well as [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]]'s series ''[[Barsoom]]'', [[C. S. Lewis]]'s novel ''[[Out of the Silent Planet]]'' (1938), and a number of [[Robert A. Heinlein]] stories before the mid-sixties. Since then, depictions of Martians have also extended to animation. A comic figure of an intelligent Martian, [[Marvin the Martian]], appeared in ''[[Haredevil Hare]]'' (1948) as a character in the [[Looney Tunes]] animated cartoons of [[Warner Brothers]], and has continued as part of popular culture to the present. After the [[Mariner program|''Mariner'']] and [[Viking program|''Viking'']] spacecraft had returned pictures of Mars as a lifeless and canal-less world, these ideas about Mars were abandoned; for many science-fiction authors, the new discoveries initially seemed like a constraint, but eventually the post-''Viking'' knowledge of Mars became itself a source of inspiration for works like [[Kim Stanley Robinson]]'s [[Mars trilogy|''Mars'' trilogy]].{{Cite book |last=Crossley |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v3TDEDfEPdEC |title=Imagining Mars: A Literary History |date=3 January 2011 |publisher=Wesleyan University Press |isbn=978-0-8195-7105-2 |pages=xiii-xiv |language=en}} == See also == * [[Astronomy on Mars]] * {{Annotated link|Outline of Mars}} * {{Annotated link|List of missions to Mars}} * {{Annotated link|Magnetic field of Mars}} * {{Annotated link|Mineralogy of Mars}} == Notes == {{reflist |group=caption}} {{notelist |notes= {{efn | name=best-fit ellipsoid | Best-fit [[ellipsoid]]}} }} == References == {{cite journal |last=Andert |first=T.
